newsitem.title: USA: World still dangerous, Cohen warns Americans.
newsitem.headline: World still dangerous, Cohen warns Americans.

text.p: New U.S. Defense Secretary William Cohen said on Friday his top priority will be to persuade Americans lulled by peace that the world is still dangerous.

"We still live in a very dangerous, disorderly world. And in many cases we face dangers that are comparable to those we faced in the past," he told reporters, citing the growth of terrorism, missile technology, and weapons of mass destruction.

Cohen, who will present the fiscal 1998 defense budget of about $260 billion to Congress next week, told his first Pentagon news conference since being sworn in last week that Americans must realize danger didn't die with the Cold War.

"My greatest concern is that we be able to persuade the American people that having a viable, sustainable national security policy is important, even when there is no clearly identifiable enemy on the horizon," he said.

"We have to do that on a bipartisan basis and persuade the American people that we remain militarily strong, that we remain forward deployed and that we remain energetically and diplomatically engaged."

Cohen, 56, who retired this month as a U.S. senator from Maine following 24 years in Congress, is the only Republican in President Bill Clinton's Cabinet. On Capitol Hill, he had a reputation as a moderate compromiser.

He reiterated in response to questions that the 8,500 U.S. military peacekeepers now serving in Bosnia should leave by the end of their current 18-month deadline in mid-1998 whether or not Europe decides that further peacekeeping is needed there.
And he defended the administration's recent moves to improve relations with China despite differences with Beijing's Communist leaders over human rights, trade and other issues.

"I think we are better off and are in a better position to help influence (Chinese) behavior over a longer period of time by being constructively engaged -- even though on a short term we may not see much progress," Cohen said.

The new secretary suggested that he personally favored lifting a virtual embargo against sales of frontline U.S. arms to Latin America on a case-by-case basis, although he stressed that Clinton had made no decision on the matter yet.
"With respect to Latin America, I have not had an opportunity to really study what the implications are," Cohen told reporters.

"To the extent that there are democracies that are now burgeoning in Latin America, to the extent that we now see civilian control over the military and to the extent that we can through arms sales have a closer relationship with those countries, then I think you can make the case that they ought to proceed on an ad hoc basis," he said.
